Perplexity vs ChatGPT for Research: Audit the Sources

Both signed-in services linked supporting primary sources for our seven requested facts. Start with ordinary Search and inspect the passages behind important claims before paying. Perplexity required sign-in in our anonymous attempt, and an extra ChatGPT date qualification still needed clarification.

What happened in the trial

One prompt asked about JSON requirements, three Apollo 11 event dates and Python dictionary ordering. We checked seven requested facts against the original RFC, NASA pages and pinned Python 3.14 documentation.

AttemptObserved result
Perplexity, signed outReturned “Sign up and repeat your request.” No research answer to score.
Perplexity, signed inSeven requested facts matched the references; three inline primary-source links returned.
ChatGPT, ordinary new chatSeven requested facts matched the references; three primary-source links returned.
ChatGPT, Web search selectedSeven requested facts matched the references; three primary-source links returned, with a different NASA page.

The second ChatGPT answer also said the landing date was “not the first-step date.” Its cited NASA page lists launch, landing and Earth-return timestamps, but does not state the first-step timing. That added qualification needs a source and timezone; it does not make all seven requested facts wrong.

Perplexity displayed a count of six sources but exposed three inline destinations for the three answer parts. ChatGPT returned three visible source links. Those interface counts are not directly comparable measures of accuracy or distinct publishers.

This is a small source-trail check. It does not establish which service is generally more accurate, faster or better on a paid plan.

Run the same research questions

  1. In Perplexity, select Search. If the request asks for sign-in, decide whether to use an account under the current terms; an access block is not an incorrect research answer.
  2. In ChatGPT web, use Add → Web search when you want to choose search explicitly. Keep that selection while entering the question. Record the plan and any visible model label.
  3. Submit the same question text. Save the first answer and its actual link destinations before requesting corrections.
  4. Open each important source. Check the exact passage, event, version, date and timezone needed by the claim, then record supported, unsupported or unavailable evidence below.
Full research prompt
Search the web and answer the three questions below in English. Use primary sources only: RFC Editor/IETF, NASA, and the Python 3.14 documentation. Give a clickable source link immediately after each numbered answer. Use your own words; do not quote source sentences. Keep the whole answer under 180 words. If the required source cannot be opened or does not establish a claim, say so instead of inventing a citation.

1. Under RFC 8259, can a JSON text consist only of the number 42? Does the standard say object member names MUST be unique or SHOULD be unique? Preserve that distinction.
2. According to NASA, what are the Apollo 11 launch, lunar-landing and splashdown dates? Label the three events separately; do not substitute the date of a first step for the landing.
3. In Python 3.14 documentation, since which Python version is dictionary insertion order guaranteed, and does updating an existing key change its position?

Please actually search for the sources rather than answering only from memory.

For your own work, replace the questions with a small task you can independently verify. Ask for original studies, standards or official documentation where those sources are appropriate, and ask the service to say when it cannot establish an answer.

Keep a claim-to-source audit

The worksheet stays in your browser and does not fetch source pages or judge facts automatically. Your review status, source URL and notes are saved together. Download before leaving, open the saved JSON to check it, and import it to continue later.

“Not supported” means the linked page does not establish that claim as written; it does not automatically mean the claim is false. “Unavailable” records a page you could not inspect. Both need a reason, rather than a guess based on a familiar hostname.

If a request is blocked

If Perplexity asks you to sign up and repeat the request, signing in and resubmitting is a separate attempt. Keep the blocked attempt in your notes. Do not treat a visible search box as proof that the anonymous request will finish.

A model-selection or plan prompt does not by itself show that you need to subscribe for a simple lookup. Return to ordinary Search and check the options available to your account. We did not purchase a subscription or test paid quotas.

If a cited page is missing, requires access or does not contain the claimed evidence, mark that limitation and seek another original source. Keep the answer and the corrected citation separately; a new link does not retroactively verify the original one.

Test conditions and limits

On November 25, 2026, Perplexity’s anonymous Search attempt produced only a sign-up request. A new Search request on a signed-in Free account then completed. ChatGPT was also signed in on Free; one ordinary run and one fresh run with Web search selected used the same question text. The underlying model identifiers were not established. These runs were not simultaneous or a matched-model experiment.

We inspected visible answers, link destinations and supporting source passages. We did not retain internal retrieval-call receipts, so a displayed link is not proof of a particular internal browsing action. UI mode selection, answer completion, source availability and factual support are different observations.

The test covers seven stable factual checks, not a representative benchmark, a latency measurement or an academic-reference evaluation. It does not compare Computer agents, Deep Research, paid models or every account region. For supplied-text tasks without web research, see the Claude and ChatGPT task trial.

Sources and original records

Official product instructions checked November 25, 2026: Perplexity Search and Pro Search and ChatGPT web search. Search behavior and availability can vary by account.

Primary references: RFC 8259, sections 2 and 4, NASA Apollo 11 mission, NASA mission timestamps, and Python 3.14 dictionaries.
